seo.title: Karmic tail 3 22 10 compatibility: waiting for something to turn up
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 22 10 compatibility: The Empress, The Fool and The Wheel of Fortune in a couple, read through Lisovskaya, Waite and Dickens's Micawbers.

title: The 3-22-10 karmic tail in compatibility: a home, a leap and a wheel
short: The Empress, The Fool and The Wheel of Fortune turn up together in compatibility for roughly one couple in 111. It is the tail of a union that wants a home and plenty (3), travels towards it light, from despair to cheerfulness in half an hour (22), and has one thing to learn: not to wait for the wheel to turn by itself (10). The riddle sits in the middle: neither partner has The Fool in their personal tail; it is born only in the couple. And the most exact portrait of such a union was written by Dickens: Mr and Mrs Micawber, whose motto is "in case anything turned up".

sections.h2: The riddle: a Fool that neither partner has
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's tail is the sum of the same points in two personal charts. So for any of its cards one can find out what it is made of. The 3-22-10 tail can be assembled in only two ways, and both say the same thing.

In 97% of such couples one partner has the personal tail 12-16-4 and the other 18-6-6. The entry is built from 12 and 18 (30 → 3), the middle from 16 and 6, the main task from 4 and 6. Neither The Empress, nor The Fool, nor The Wheel appears in these people's personal tails. Another 3% of couples have the personal tails 21-10-7 and 9-12-3: here the partners already carry The Wheel and The Empress, but still not The Fool — it is made from 10 and 12.

So the lightness with which this couple jumps from trouble to celebration is not "his" trait or "hers". It is weather that the two create only together. When one blames the other for being careless, the tail disagrees: neither partner has The Fool in their personal tail.

The second oddity is arithmetic. In a personal chart the middle of the tail equals the sum of its ends, and between 3 and 10 there would stand 13, Death. In a couple the middle is added up from the middles of two people, so the result is 22. As a personal tail the triple 3-22-10 does not exist: no single person has this story, only a union does.
Dickens noticed this long before any matrix. Having described Mr Micawber weeping at supper and then planning an extension at bedtime, he added one sentence: "And Mrs. Micawber was just the same."

sections.h2: The Micawbers: a family waiting for something to turn up
paragraphs: In David Copperfield (1849–1850) young David lodges with the Micawbers in London. The centre of the street door is covered with "a great brass-plate, on which was engraved 'Mrs. Micawber's Boarding Establishment for Young Ladies'". Only, Dickens writes, "I never found that any young lady had ever been to school there; or that any young lady ever came, or proposed to come". Creditors came instead.

Mr Micawber could "come home to supper with a flood of tears, and a declaration that nothing was now left but a jail", and then "go to bed making a calculation of the expense of putting bow-windows to the house, 'in case anything turned up', which was his favourite expression". Mrs Micawber could be "thrown into fainting fits by the king's taxes at three o'clock, and to eat lamb chops, breaded, and drink warm ale (paid for with two tea-spoons that had gone to the pawnbroker's) at four". She almost always had one of the twins in her arms.

Then come the debtors' prison and release under the Insolvent Debtors Act, Plymouth, where the relations received them coolly, coal on the River Medway, Canterbury, corn on commission, service under Uriah Heep, the exposure of Heep and, at last, Australia. And through all of it runs one sentence of Mrs Micawber's, repeated at every turn: "I never will desert Mr. Micawber."

The Micawbers are not invented. Dickens drew them from his own parents. His father, John Dickens, was imprisoned for debt in London's Marshalsea in 1824, and there he told his twelve-year-old son the very rule Micawber would later repeat: twenty pounds a year in income and nineteen pounds nineteen shillings and sixpence spent is happiness, a shilling the other way is wretchedness. His mother, Elizabeth Dickens, decided to save the family with a school, and a brass plate reading "Mrs. Dickens's Establishment" appeared on the door of a house in Gower Street. "Yet nobody ever came to school," Dickens recalled in the autobiographical fragment published by his friend and biographer John Forster. "Under similar disguises my own father and mother are in my books," Dickens admitted himself. And later he said of his father: "The longer I live, the better man I think him."

This matters for reading the tail. The Micawbers are funny, but they are written with love, and there is no culprit in their story. Nor are there roles by gender: in a 3-22-10 couple either partner can turn out to be "Mr Micawber", and more often both take turns. The novel is not a forecast but a mirror: it shows how the circle works and how they got out of it.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Empress and the language of home
paragraphs: Lisovskaya calls this point what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". And she warns that the point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also become resistance. On the site this couple sees The Empress twice: at the entry to the tail and in the sphere "Relationship and common language".

The Micawbers' common language is the language of home. There is nothing to eat, and Mrs Micawber talks about the larder: "I was accustomed to speak of the larder when I lived with papa and mama, and I use the word almost unconsciously. What I mean to express is, that there is nothing to eat in the house." Mr Micawber has his eye on a terrace fronting Hyde Park and wonders where to throw out a bow-window or carry up the roof another storey. Twins, boarding school, bow-window, terrace — all of it is The Empress, the wish for a full cup. On this subject the two never argue.

Wen has a short formula for The Empress: "She produces. She makes things happen." The Micawbers' brass plate is The Empress turned inside out: the sign of a home instead of a home, the board of a school nobody will ever attend. Wen describes The Empress reversed almost as this scene: "Efforts of creation and innovation won't yield results. There is a sense of emptiness and no production after much work and effort."

But the main clue lies in Waite's divinatory list. For The Empress it begins brightly: "Fruitfulness, action, initiative, length of days". And it ends in shadow: "the unknown, clandestine; also difficulty, doubt, ignorance". Now Mrs Micawber, on the evening the court released her husband: "Mr. Micawber may have concealed his difficulties from me in the first instance… I do not deny that he has kept me in the dark as to his resources and his liabilities both." **Concealed, difficulties, in the dark: the shadow half of one card in one speech.** In the novel "difficulties" is the family word for debts: "When I lived at home with papa and mama, I really should have hardly understood what the word meant, in the sense in which I now employ it."

This is how the entry becomes resistance. A 3-22-10 couple talks easily about the home, and that is exactly why the home is such a convenient place to hide the bills. An evening on the sofa: the two choose kitchen tiles for a flat whose first instalment has not yet been paid, and it is a happy evening. Nobody raises the overdue payment: it would spoil the language in which they feel so good. In Lisovskaya, The Empress's tasks for a couple include surviving "feast or famine", learning to be practical and getting out from under the relatives' influence. With the Micawbers all three appear in a single chapter: feast and famine on the same day, a boarding school without a single pupil instead of a business, and "my family" deciding where they should go.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: The Fool, or elasticity
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya this point has no meaning of its own: it is an addition to the main task. The site reads it as the path — what the couple does and goes through between the wish and the task. This is our reading, and in 3-22-10 the path runs through The Fool.

Dickens found the exact word for it: elasticity. After a creditor's visit Mr Micawber "would be transported with grief and mortification", "but within half-an-hour afterwards, he would polish up his shoes with extraordinary pains, and go out, humming a tune". On the day of his arrest he told David that "the God of day had now gone down upon him" — "But I heard, afterwards, that he was seen to play a lively game at skittles, before noon." The Fool measures distance in his own way: Micawber set off for Canterbury as if for the farthest limits of the earth, and for Australia as if for a little trip across the Channel. "The distance is quite imaginary."

Waite calls The Fool "the spirit in search of experience", and in the divinatory list puts first "Folly, mania, extravagance". Mrs Micawber, without disowning her husband, admits exactly this: "I do not deny that he is improvident." Lisovskaya describes The Fool in a couple with the same two sides. With him it is easy to start from nothing, find a way out, laugh, set off on the road. It is hard when it comes to serious steps that need boundaries and responsibility. A 3-22-10 couple recognises itself in both halves. Three moves in five years, and every time "this one is for good". The last money spent on a celebration because "we deserve it". Laughter on the hardest evening, which has saved the union more than once.

The Fool also has a leap. Micawber uses the word himself: "You find me, fallen back, FOR a spring; and I have every reason to believe that a vigorous leap will shortly be the result." Wen places The Fool at the edge of a cliff: the next step "could either send the Seeker flying into the air over that cliff with impressive accomplishment or falling down hard from naïveté"; before him is a choice "between two forks in the path". The Micawbers leapt twice, and the novel shows both forks. The first leap was an advertisement in all the papers, "Now employ me, on remunerative terms", paid for with a new bill; Uriah Heep answered it. The second was Australia. What separates one leap from the other is something a 3-22-10 couple spends its whole life finding out, and the answer lies in the main task.

sections.h2: Main task: the Wheel they wait for
paragraphs: Lisovskaya reads the main task mostly through its downside: what does not work for the couple and what it has to learn. The Wheel of Fortune in a couple means cycles: rises and falls follow each other, and the struggle is not with the change itself but with how the couple meets it. On the downside: a seesaw of "silence and conflict", life in debt, the habit of blaming fate, the feeling that being together is hard and yet something holds them.

Micawber's motto is a ready formula for this downside. In English it reads "in case anything turned up", and "turn up" is also what a card does when it is turned over from the pack: to "turn up trumps". In the same chapter Dickens himself slips into the language of cards: Micawber goes in for "anything that might be on the cards". The Russian translators, A. V. Krivtsova and Yevgeny Lann, rendered it "esli schastye ulybnyotsya", "if happiness smiles". And happiness, felicity, is the last word in Waite's list for the Wheel: "Destiny, fortune, success, elevation, luck, felicity." **In both languages the couple's motto is a Wheel that is supposed to turn by itself.**
Yet Waite explains the Wheel the other way round: behind the symbol, he writes, "there lies the denial of chance". The Micawbers live as if there were nothing but chance.

Wen compares the wheel to the unit circle of trigonometry: sine and cosine reveal "the philosophy of oscillations between zeniths and nadirs". With the Micawbers the oscillation can be read off the clock: fainting at three, lamb chops at four. It even has an exact amplitude — the famous rule: "Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure nineteen nineteen and six, result happiness. Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure twenty pounds ought and six, result misery." Between happiness and misery lies one shilling. On the downside a 3-22-10 couple lives exactly on this line and keeps stepping over it by sixpence.

The most exact scene of the downside is the day of release from prison. David expects a celebration, but the Micawbers are inconsolable: "Mr. and Mrs. Micawber were so used to their old difficulties, I think, that they felt quite shipwrecked when they came to consider that they were released from them." **This is the Wheel's trap: the seesaw becomes home.** A quiet month feels suspicious, a quarrel and reconciliation feel like proof of love, and money enters the conversation only when the bank calls. And the one to blame is always someone else: the Custom House, where "they would rather NOT have a man of Mr. Micawber's abilities", the relations in Plymouth, society. The Micawbers never blame each other — that is their strength. But they blame fate all the time.

sections.h2: The turn: "assist to turn them up"
paragraphs: The formula for the way out comes from Mrs Micawber, in the chapter called "Mr. Micawber's Gauntlet": "I am convinced, myself, and this I have pointed out to Mr. Micawber several times of late, that things cannot be expected to turn up of themselves. We must, in a measure, assist to turn them up." **This is the main task of the 3-22-10 tail in one sentence: from "in case anything turned up" to "assist to turn them up".**

But the first attempt fails, and the novel shows honestly why. Mrs Micawber's way of assisting is to throw down the gauntlet to society, advertise in all the papers and, since advertising is expensive, raise the money "on a bill". It is still waiting, only louder, and still debt. The gauntlet was taken up by Uriah Heep. Micawber sends David a solemn letter: "something has turned up". Later he reads aloud a different letter: his salary from Heep was "the pittance of twenty-two shillings and six per week", the advances from Heep "were secured by I.O.U.'s", "And that I thus became immeshed in the web he had spun for my reception?" What turned up by itself turned out to be a hook.

Micawber gets out of the web not by chance but by an act: he gathers evidence against Heep and exposes him in front of everyone. The secret that held him stops being a secret. After that David's aunt suggests Australia. Mrs Micawber asks whether there will be room for her husband's talents, and hears that there is "no better opening anywhere, for a man who conducts himself well, and is industrious". She repeats the words like a formula: "Precisely." And before sailing she says the main thing: "I wish Mr. Micawber… to be the Caesar of his own fortunes."

How it all ended Dickens reports through an Australian newspaper. Micawber worked in the Bush so hard that, in Mr Peggotty's words, his bald head was "a perspiring in the sun… till I a'most thowt it would have melted away"; in the original Peggotty's highest praise is that he "turned to with a will" (the Russian translation drops the phrase). He paid off every debt he had left in England, "even to Traddles's bill". Now he is Port Middlebay District Magistrate, and in his speech at a public dinner he warns the young against the shoals of "pecuniary liabilities which they were unable to liquidate".

The Wheel turned after the couple stopped waiting for it. The strong version of the 3-22-10 tail loses neither The Empress nor The Fool: in Australia the Micawbers still love dinners, songs and fine words, and the family is as big and noisy as ever — at the dinner in the father's honour the son sings. Only one thing changes: who turns the wheel.

sections.h2: Centre and values: the family court and the choice that gets reread
paragraphs: Every couple with this tail has 20, Judgement, at the centre. The centre of a couple is the atmosphere inside the union, what is not on show. In Lisovskaya the key to Judgement in a couple is lineage and family: relatives, traditions, the influence of parents.

In the Micawbers' home this court sits all the time. "My family" is what Mrs Micawber calls her relations, and she "always said those two words with an air, though I never could discover who came under the denomination". The family decides that Mr Micawber must go to Plymouth, the family recommends coal, the family does not answer letters. "Papa and mama" keep coming up in her speech. Even the wedding was hurried by papa's maxim "never do tomorrow what you can do today", and Micawber sighs that the marriage "was so far prematurely entered into, in consequence, that I never recovered the expense". The downside of Judgement in a couple is living under the relatives' eye and checking every decision against their verdict. The upside sounds on the last evening before sailing, when Mrs Micawber speaks of her children's children: "However vigorous the sapling, I cannot forget the parent-tree." The family stops being a judge and becomes a root.
The couple's values are another answer to the question of what this union is for. In 73% of such couples this point holds The Lovers, in 27% The Devil.

The Lovers are a choice. Before leaving for Canterbury Mrs Micawber tells how, the night before, she read the marriage service over by candlelight, with the words "I, Emma, take thee, Wilkins", and drew her conclusion: "that I never could desert Mr. Micawber". A choice made once she makes again — from the text, like an exam. When The Lovers stand in the values, the union rests on this repeated "yes".

The Devil is what binds. Young David kept hearing about a certain "Deed" in the Micawber house and was "conscious of having confounded it with those demoniacal parchments which are held to have, once upon a time, obtained to a great extent in Germany". Then came the I.O.U.s and Heep's "web". If The Devil stands in the values, the couple has to tell two kinds of ties apart: those that hold them together and those that hold them on a leash.

These couples have the twentieth arcanum at the centre, and Micawber's rule starts with twenty pounds. Heep paid him twenty-two shillings and sixpence a week — for the leap that turned into a fall — and the couple's Fool carries the number 22. Mrs Micawber once declares that her husband has "the judicial mind", and the novel ends with him becoming a magistrate — under a centre called Judgement. Dickens knew nothing of the destiny matrix, and no conclusions are drawn from these numbers here. But they are hard not to notice.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with the 3-22-10 tail
paragraphs: Not a recipe, but what can be seen in the cards themselves and in the novel:

ul: **Name your own "twenty pounds".** The month's sum and the line beyond which debt begins are shared knowledge, not one person's secret.
**Do not keep each other "in the dark".** Talk about money on a schedule, once a month, not when the bank calls. The Empress is strong when her house stands on the truth.

**Check the fork before the leap.** An advertisement on borrowed money and a ticket to Australia with a plan of work are both leaps. There is one question: is this a step towards the work or one more way of waiting?
**Assist things to turn up.** One concrete step a week instead of "if only": call, send, count.
**Do not mistake the seesaw for closeness.** A calm month is not a shipwreck. If the two are bored without a crisis, that is the Wheel's habit, not a measure of love.
**Keep the lightness.** Laughter and the knack of starting from nothing are this couple's strength. They need no correcting, only a direction.
**Keep the promise "I never will desert" — but not as a vow of silence.** Loyalty and honesty about the bills do not get in each other's way.

paragraphs: If the debts no longer fit into the family budget, that is work for a lawyer or a financial adviser, not for waiting. Micawber, too, was let out of prison not by chance but by the Insolvent Debtors Act.

A couple's tail is not recalculated from its two end numbers: each of its points is added up from the same points of two personal charts and reduced to 22. A person born on 14.04.1975 has the personal tail 12-16-4, a person born on 04.07.1975 has 18-6-6.

If the middle were calculated by the personal formula, it would be 3 + 10 = 13, Death. In a couple it is added up from the middles of two people: 16 + 6 = 22. This couple's centre is 20 (8 + 12), Judgement, and its values are The Lovers.

This tail has no permutations: among couples' tails the numbers 3, 22 and 10 occur only in this order. But it has two neighbours with the same ends. By our count over all dates from 1900 to 2025, the tail 3-4-10 occurs in about 1% of couples and 3-13-10 in 0.44%. All three share one wish, a home and plenty, and one task, keeping their footing on the Wheel. The road differs: through The Emperor's order, through Death's ending of the old, or through The Fool's leap.

The Fool in the middle of a couple's tail is rare in general: it stands there in about 4 couples out of 100, and only five tails have it. In 3-22-10 it is especially striking, because neither partner has it in their personal tail.

ul: Charles Dickens, David Copperfield (1849–1850): chapters 11–12, 17, 27–28, 52, 57 and 63; the Russian translation by A. V. Krivtsova and Yevgeny Lann for the Russian wording of the motto.
John Forster, The Life of Charles Dickens (1872–1874), volume I: Dickens's autobiographical fragment on the Marshalsea and the school in Gower Street.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910): The Empress, The Fool, The Wheel of Fortune.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): The Empress, The Fool, The Wheel of Fortune.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of a couple's points, energies 3, 10, 20 and 22.
Frequencies and combinations: a run over all dates with the site's engine.

**3 · The Empress — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: a home, a full larder, a family, growth. It is also their common language: the two agree most easily when they talk about the home.

**22 · The Fool — middle of the task.** How the couple moves towards the goal: lightly, in leaps, with moves and fresh starts from nothing. The lightness rescues them in a crisis and fails them when a long stride is needed.

**10 · The Wheel of Fortune — main task.** Ups and downs follow each other in this couple. The task is to stop waiting for the turn and learn to turn the wheel themselves, without letting go of each other's hands.

faq.q: What does the 3-22-10 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: These are the couple's tasks in three cards. The Empress at the entry is the shared wish for a home, plenty and a family. The Fool in the middle is a light path of leaps and fresh starts. The Wheel of Fortune as the main task is learning to go through ups and downs together without waiting for things to sort themselves out.

faq.q: Why is The Fool in the middle if 3 + 10 = 13?
faq.a: That is how a personal tail is calculated. In a couple's chart each point is the sum of the same points of two people, and the middle is added up from their middles: for example, 16 + 6 = 22. That is why a single person never has the 3-22-10 tail.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail shows a task, not a verdict. On its downside it resembles the Micawbers' life on the seesaw, on its upside their Australia: the same lightness and the same full house, but they turn the wheel themselves.
No. The cards do not establish anyone's financial situation. The Wheel speaks of change and of how the couple meets it, and money is simply where this shows most often.

faq.q: Who plays Mr Micawber in the couple?
faq.a: Either partner, or both by turns. The cards do not assign roles by gender, and in this tail neither partner has The Fool on their own — it belongs to both.

unit.meaning: Your task is not to wait for things to turn up by themselves but to help them: talk honestly about money and act.
